passage:
Honeybees cannot speak, yet a forager returning to the hive can tell her sisters exactly where she found nectar. In the 1940s, the Austrian zoologist Karl von Frisch decoded the method: a behaviour now called the waggle dance.

On the vertical honeycomb, in darkness, the returning bee performs a figure-of-eight run. The straight middle section — the "waggle run" — is the message. Its angle relative to straight up on the comb encodes the angle of the food source relative to the sun outside: straight up means "fly toward the sun", straight down means "fly away from the sun". The duration of the waggle run encodes distance — roughly, the longer the waggle, the farther the food.

Followers crowd around the dancer, touching her with their antennae to read the vibrations, and several will then fly out and find the same patch of flowers. Remarkably, the dance is graded: a rich, nearby source triggers a long, vigorous performance that recruits many foragers, while a poor source earns only a brief, half-hearted shuffle — or no dance at all. The colony therefore allocates its workforce almost like a market, sending more bees to the best discoveries.

Von Frisch's work, which earned him a share of the 1973 Nobel Prize, showed that an insect brain smaller than a grain of rice can perform something close to symbolic communication — conveying direction, distance, and even quality through movement alone.
